lead: ARM is a RISC processor family. An ARM7-class core has sixteen visible 32-bit registers, a current status register, saved status copies in exception modes, and a three-stage pipeline. The design keeps instructions simple and fast, and lets an interrupt or fault switch to a private register bank quickly. You meet it in phone chips, car controllers, routers and microcontroller boards. This chapter covers the visible registers, the processor modes, and why the program counter reads ahead.
prereq: You need: the pipeline idea from Chapter 2.2 and RISC versus CISC from Unit 1.

blocks.text: An ARM7TDMI implements the ARMv4T architecture. The name packs features: ARM7 core, Thumb, debug support and a multiplier. ARMv4T defines two instruction states: 32-bit ARM state and 16-bit Thumb state. The T bit in the status register selects the state.

An ARM7TDMI in ARM state sees sixteen 32-bit registers, R0 to R15. Each holds one 32-bit word. R0 to R12 are general purpose: arithmetic, load/store and address work use them freely. Three have agreed roles. R13 is the stack pointer (SP): it holds the address of the top of the current stack. R14 is the link register (LR): a branch with link writes the return address there. R15 is the program counter (PC): it holds the address of the instruction being fetched. SP, LR and PC are conventions; the hardware treats them as R13, R14 and R15.

Two status registers matter. The current program status register (CPSR) holds condition flags and control bits for the running program. The saved program status register (SPSR) holds a copy of CPSR when an exception occurs; it exists only in exception modes, not in User or System mode. Four CPSR flags record the last result: N means negative, Z means zero, C means carry or borrow, and V means signed overflow. Control bits include I, which disables IRQ when set, F, which disables FIQ when set, and T, which selects Thumb state when set. T = 0 means 32-bit ARM state.

An ARM7 core has seven processor modes. User mode runs normal application code. FIQ mode handles the fast interrupt. IRQ mode handles the normal interrupt. Supervisor mode runs after reset and handles software interrupts. Abort mode handles a failed memory access. Undefined mode handles an unknown instruction. System mode is privileged and uses the User register bank; an operating system uses it to run privileged code without a mode switch.

Each exception mode has private copies of some registers. These are banked registers. In FIQ, IRQ, Supervisor, Abort and Undefined modes, R13 and R14 are banked, and an SPSR exists. FIQ also banks R8 to R12. User and System share the same R13, R14 and general registers and have no SPSR.

When an exception is taken, the core switches mode, copies CPSR into that mode's SPSR, saves the return address in that mode's LR, and starts at a fixed vector. The handler can use its private R13 as a stack pointer and R14 for return, so it need not save the User bank first. FIQ goes further: its private R8-R12 let a short handler work without saving those registers. Interrupt priority and latency belong to Unit 3.

ARM7 uses a three-stage pipeline: fetch, decode, execute. Fetch reads the next instruction from memory. Decode works out what it means. Execute does the operation. In steady state, three instructions are in the pipeline at once, one in each stage.

Because fetch runs ahead, the PC value during an instruction is not that instruction's address. In ARM state, PC = address of executing instruction + 8 bytes. The +8 is two 32-bit words: the instruction being fetched is two words ahead. In Thumb state, instructions are 16 bits, so PC = executing address + 4 bytes. The offset is in bytes, not instruction count. A branch writes its target into PC; the pipeline must refill, so useful work is lost.
PC = A + 8 (ARM state); PC = A + 4 (Thumb state)
blocks.where: PC is the value read through R15; A is the byte address of the executing instruction. ARM state uses 4-byte instructions; Thumb state uses 2-byte instructions.

blocks.text: Newer ARM cores in the Cortex series keep these ideas but add deeper pipelines, caches and more modes. Only a few universities teach that detail at this depth.

figure.caption: Instructions I1, I2 and I3 overlap by one cycle per stage. For I1 at 0x00002000, when I1 is in execute, I3 is in fetch, so the PC reads 0x00002008.

examples.question: An ARM7TDMI runs in ARM state. It executes an instruction at byte address 0x00002000. Give the value read from the PC and the addresses of the instructions in the decode and fetch stages. Use byte addresses.
steps: In ARM state, PC read = executing address + 8 bytes.
Decode stage holds the next instruction, one word ahead: A + 4 = 0x00002004 = 8196.
Fetch stage holds the instruction being fetched, at the PC value: 0x00002008 = 8200.
examples.answer: The executing instruction is at 0x00002000 (8192), the decode-stage instruction at 0x00002004 (8196), and the PC/fetch-stage address is 0x00002008 (8200), all byte addresses.

traps: PC is not the address of the executing instruction. In ARM state it is executing address + 8 bytes; in Thumb state + 4 bytes.
SPSR exists only in exception modes. User and System mode have CPSR only.
FIQ banks R8-R12 as well as R13, R14 and SPSR. IRQ does not bank R8-R12.
R13, R14 and R15 are not hardwired names; SP, LR and PC are programmer conventions.
The +8 and +4 offsets are byte counts, not instruction counts. Do not add 8 instructions.

quiz.q: Name R13, R14 and R15 by their usual roles.
quiz.a: R13 is the stack pointer, R14 is the link register, R15 is the program counter.

quiz.q: Which CPSR bit selects Thumb state, and what value means Thumb?
quiz.a: The T bit. T = 1 means Thumb state; T = 0 means ARM state.

quiz.q: Why does an FIQ handler usually need fewer register saves than an IRQ handler?
quiz.a: FIQ mode banks R8-R12 in addition to R13, R14 and SPSR. IRQ mode banks only R13, R14 and SPSR.

quiz.q: Why does User mode have no SPSR?
quiz.a: SPSR is written when an exception is taken. User mode is not an exception mode, so it has CPSR only.

quiz.q: In ARM state, an instruction at byte address 0x00004000 is executing. What PC value is read, and what address sits in decode?
In Thumb state, an instruction at byte address 0x00001000 is executing. What PC value is read?
A student says PC reads 0x00002004 for an ARM-state instruction at 0x00002000. Identify the mistake and give the correct PC.
quiz.a: The student added 4, the Thumb offset or the decode-stage address. ARM state uses +8 bytes, so PC = 0x00002008; 0x00002004 is the decode-stage instruction.

quiz.q: Explain why banked R13 is useful on exception entry.
quiz.a: The handler gets a private stack pointer at once. It can push return data without overwriting the interrupted program's stack, so entry is faster and safer.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern ARM cores in the Cortex-M and Cortex-A families add caches, branch prediction and deeper pipelines; Cortex-M cores target microcontrollers while Cortex-A cores run Linux. TrustZone adds a secure and non-secure world for payment and key storage. Search next for Cortex-M register bank, exception entry and branch penalty.
